evidence.claim: USFD, DPZ, OLO, QSR, and WING score highest in this candidate chunk by Serenity priority because they combine clearer public-market mapping with falsifiable exposure to distribution, digital infrastructure, franchised unit economics, value/traffic durability, or commodity-sensitive throughput.

memory_update.content: For the Restaurants theme, prioritize USFD, DPZ, OLO, QSR, and WING for next-step evidence collection. These names best map to Serenity chokepoints: foodservice distribution/cost control, digital ordering and delivery, restaurant software/payments, franchised QSR economics, and digital/unit-growth QSR models.
WING duplicate candidate was removed from the ranked universe; Wingstop appears only once.
WBT / Manitowoc / Welbilt equipment exposure is not a validated ticker mapping and should be treated as a placeholder until public-market equipment exposure is re-mapped.

Layer 4 should verify latest 10-K/10-Q, earnings call, investor presentation, and segment KPIs for the top five candidates, focusing on traffic versus price, franchisee unit economics, digital/payment attach, distributor case volume, private-label penetration, and commodity/labor margin bridges.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest filings/earnings evidence for independent restaurant case growth, exclusive-brand mix, gross-margin bridge, customer retention, and whether menu-engineering tools are driving measurable share gains rather than normal distribution volume.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Best Serenity-style chokepoint candidate in this chunk because it sits between restaurant operators and food/input cost pressure. If restaurants face persistent labor, commodity, and menu-pricing constraints, a broadline distributor with scale, private/exclusive brands, purchasing data, menu tools, and operator services may be a cleaner way to study cost-control demand than any single restaurant brand. Public-market purity is high because foodservice distribution is the core business, and the thesis is highly falsifiable through case volume, independent restaurant demand, gross margin, private-label penetration, and operator retention.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need separation of traffic/order growth from price/mix, plus evidence that delivery aggregators, carryout value offers, and loyalty are strengthening franchisee economics rather than relying on promotion intensity.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: High-priority operator because Domino's directly tests several restaurant funnel nodes at once: delivery/carryout frequency, digital ordering, franchisee economics, value positioning, and food/labor cost pass-through. The business is highly mapped to the public market, and the key thesis can be tested through same-store sales, order counts, ticket, franchisee profitability, delivery economics, loyalty/digital mix, and unit growth.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need validation of competitive moat versus POS vendors, delivery platforms, payment processors, and in-house enterprise systems; also need proof that payments and guest-engagement modules can scale without margin dilution or customer churn.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Strong chokepoint-style software candidate because restaurant operators are prioritizing digital ordering, payments, loyalty, guest engagement, delivery-channel control, and data loops. Olo is a relatively pure public-market mapping to restaurant digital infrastructure rather than restaurant traffic alone. The opportunity is falsifiable through location count, average revenue per unit, module attach rates, payment adoption, net revenue retention, customer concentration, and competitive displacement.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need brand-level evidence separating Burger King turnaround, Tim Hortons coffee traffic, Popeyes chicken growth, and Firehouse expansion; consolidated numbers may hide uneven franchisee economics.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: High-priority franchisor platform because it tests QSR value perception, global unit growth, franchisee health, coffee frequency, burger/beef pressure, chicken exposure, remodel capex, and international expansion. Its multi-brand structure gives a broader restaurant read-through than a single-concept operator. Thesis validation is relatively clear through comparable sales, traffic, franchisee profitability, development pipeline, remodel pace, royalty growth, and margin bridge.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest evidence that same-store growth is transaction-led rather than price-led, and that franchisee returns remain attractive if chicken-wing costs normalize upward or promotional intensity rises.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Priority growth-franchise candidate because it cleanly exposes digital ordering, franchised unit growth, chicken-wing commodity sensitivity, and restaurant throughput. Its asset-light model gives a focused test of whether strong consumer frequency and franchisee returns can overcome input volatility. The thesis can be falsified through same-store sales quality, transaction growth, wing-cost changes, unit openings, franchisee cash-on-cash returns, and digital mix.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need proof that new markets can sustain mature-store sales and margins without excessive labor, real-estate, or opening-cost pressure.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Useful growth-format candidate because beverage frequency, drive-thru throughput, labor scheduling, real-estate expansion, and coffee/input inflation are direct restaurant-funnel questions. Demand durability may be stronger than meal-based concepts if habitual beverage visits persist, but the bottleneck is less supply-scarce than software or distribution. The thesis is testable through new-unit productivity, same-shop transactions, ticket, labor hours, throughput, app/loyalty mix, and store-level margins.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence that breakfast and value offers are expanding transactions profitably rather than pressuring franchisee margins amid beef and labor inflation.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Good QSR value-war candidate because Wendy's directly tests consumer price sensitivity, breakfast/daypart expansion, franchisee unit economics, beef-cost exposure, and promotional discipline. It is less differentiated as a chokepoint than USFD, Olo, or the higher-growth franchised platforms, but it has clean public-market purity and strong falsifiability through traffic, same-store sales, franchisee profitability, unit openings/closures, and commodity-cost commentary.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest traffic versus pricing mix, restaurant-level margin bridge, labor-productivity evidence, and proof that premium positioning remains resilient if consumers trade down.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Strong fast-casual test case for premium burger demand, restaurant-level margin recovery, throughput, urban/suburban traffic mix, kiosk/digital adoption, and beef-cost pressure. The public-market mapping is clean and the evidence path is straightforward. It ranks below the most compelling chokepoint candidates because it is more brand/operator-specific and less supply-scarce.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need country-level same-store sales, traffic, royalty/rent burden, capex requirements, FX sensitivity, and evidence that consumer demand is not simply inflation-driven nominal growth.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Useful international franchisee/operator candidate because it separates franchisor economics from operator-level exposure to traffic, capex, FX, local inflation, labor, and emerging-market consumer demand. It may have higher mispricing potential because many U.S.-centric restaurant screens underweight Latin America operator dynamics, but the thesis depends heavily on country-level macro and currency variables.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest evidence on traffic versus check growth, labor productivity, menu simplification, food-cost bridge, and whether margin recovery is sustainable without cutting service quality.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Good full-service/casual-dining margin candidate because it is exposed to labor intensity, menu complexity, traffic, discretionary dining behavior, and commodity sensitivity. It helps test whether casual dining can defend traffic and margin without excessive discounting. It ranks lower because supplier scarcity is limited and the thesis is more execution-sensitive than chokepoint-driven.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need franchisee-level profitability, store closure/opening trends, remodel/reinvestment requirements, and evidence that traffic recovery is not purely promotion-driven.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Relevant franchised casual-dining platform because IHOP and Applebee's test value menus, franchisee health, brand reinvestment, and lower-to-middle-income consumer pressure. Mispricing potential may be higher if market narratives over- or understate brand deterioration, but the bottleneck quality is modest. Falsification is clear through franchisee closures, traffic, promotional mix, royalty health, and development pipeline.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence on traffic quality, beef-cost mitigation, discount intensity, store-level margin recovery, and whether turnaround actions improve unit economics rather than only reducing costs temporarily.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Relevant but higher-risk casual-dining and steakhouse candidate because it directly tests beef inflation, traffic, discounting, restaurant-level margins, and turnaround execution. It has clear falsifiability and potential mispricing if beef-cost or turnaround expectations are too pessimistic or optimistic, but it is not a scarce supply-chain node.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need proof of franchisee profitability, net unit growth stabilization, traffic recovery, and sustainable value positioning without margin-destructive discounting.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Useful smaller QSR turnaround candidate because it tests value positioning, franchisee health, late-night/daypart traffic, unit closures/openings, and brand reinvestment. It may have mispricing potential because smaller restaurant platforms can re-rate sharply if unit economics stabilize, but the evidence burden is high and the competitive moat is less clear.

ranked_candidates.company: The Manitowoc Company / Welbilt exposure note
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current public-market mapping for commercial foodservice equipment exposure, including which listed companies own relevant Welbilt assets or competing equipment lines, and whether restaurant capex is materially flowing into automation/throughput equipment.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Conceptually relevant because commercial kitchen equipment, refrigeration, beverage systems, and automation are plausible restaurant productivity chokepoints. However, this candidate has a ticker/company mapping problem and should not be treated as a validated public-market candidate until the listed exposure is cleaned up. It remains a coverage-gap placeholder rather than a ranked investable research lead.

summary: Layer 3 ranks this restaurant candidate chunk by Serenity research priority, emphasizing where the restaurant theme has the clearest demand signal, chokepoint exposure, public-market mapping, evidence path, and falsification plan. Highest priority goes to names that best expose value/traffic durability, franchisee unit economics, digital ordering, labor productivity, food-cost management, or distribution leverage. This is research prioritization only, not a buy/sell recommendation.
